transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, I guess what finally made me ask for help is that I just keep forgetting all these little things I normally handle fine. Like, I'm a secretary, so I should be on top of things, right? But I'll forget to return calls, or I'll completely blank on turning in a registration form. Or I'll tell myself I need to stop for an errand on the way home, and then I just drive straight back. It's so frustrating. Actually, the drive home is always so weird anyway because they just started all that construction on I-95, and it's a total mess. I don't know why they always decide to tear up the roads right when everyone is trying to commute. My neighbor, Sarah, she was saying it took her an hour and a half just to get past the exit for the mall yesterday. Have you been stuck in that yet? It's just awful. But anyway, yeah, I just keep forgetting things.
How long have you been noticing these memory problems and difficulty concentrating? Did they start suddenly, or have they been getting worse gradually over time?

Well, I guess... I mean, I've always been a little scatterbrained, but it really got noticeably harder to manage about 15 months ago. That's when I started this evening certificate program. It's supposed to help me move up at work, you know? But the classes are so late, they go until like 9 PM on Tuesdays and Thursdays. And the instructor, Mr. Davis, he literally just reads straight from the PowerPoint slides in this total monotone voice. I mean, why even make us drive all the way to the community college if you're just going to read the slides? I could do that at home in my pajamas. 

Plus, whenever I do try to study at home, my cat, Barnaby, just plops right down on my keyboard. He's an orange tabby, a total sweetheart, but he demands so much attention the second I sit down at my desk. If I don't pet him, he starts knocking my highlighters onto the floor one by one just to watch me pick them up. It's hilarious but... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the timing. Yeah, so, about 15 months ago is when the organization stuff really started getting worse.
Before these memory and concentration problems started 15 months ago, did you have any head injuries, high fevers, infections, or significant changes in any medications you were taking?

No, nothing like that. I haven't been sick or hit my head or anything. I don't really take any medicine either, except maybe ibuprofen if I get a headache, which I do sometimes get when the weather changes. Actually, my mom gets those same weather headaches. We can always tell when a storm is coming because both of us will start rubbing our temples at the exact same time. She calls us human barometers. She used to joke that we should get jobs at the local news station predicting the weather, which honestly probably pays better than being a secretary. Have you ever noticed that? How the pressure changes just make your head feel tight right before it rains? It's so weird how the body does that. But um, yeah, no head injuries or fevers or anything.
Over these past 15 months, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sad, down, or anxious—or have the main problems just been with memory and concentration?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I've felt particularly sad or anxious or anything like that. Just... frustrated, mostly, with myself. Because I know I can do better. But mood-wise, I think I'm okay. Actually, my sister was just telling me she feels anxious all the time lately, but she has three kids under five, so I feel like that's probably normal, right? I honestly don't know how she does it. Whenever I go over there, the house is just a complete disaster zone. There are Legos everywhere—I stepped on one in my bare feet last week and I swear it was the worst pain of my life. Do you have kids? Because if you do, you probably know the Lego pain. It's like a rite of passage or something. But yeah, no, I'm not sad or anxious, just having trouble keeping things straight.

Besides the memory and concentration problems, have you noticed any other changes in your physical health over the past 15 months—like unusual fatigue, sleep changes, weight changes, or any other physical symptoms that feel different from your normal baseline?

Um, physical health changes? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm pretty tired a lot, but I feel like I've always been kind of tired. Especially since I started that evening class, like I mentioned. By the time I get home, it's so late, and then I have to wind down. I usually watch a little TV, maybe some of those home renovation shows? I love those. It's amazing how they can take a totally wrecked house and make it look like a magazine cover in, like, an hour of television time. Though I know it takes months in real life. My uncle actually tried to renovate his own kitchen once, just watching YouTube videos. He completely messed up the plumbing and flooded the whole downstairs. It was a disaster. They had to live with my aunt's parents for six weeks while it got fixed. Can you imagine living with your in-laws for that long? I'd probably lose my mind. But, um... what were you asking? Oh, right, physical stuff. No, my sleep and weight and all that is pretty much the same as always. Just the usual tiredness from being busy, I guess.

When you're trying to focus on something—like reading an email or listening to someone talk—do you find that your mind just wanders away, or do you have trouble keeping your attention on it even when you really want to concentrate?

Yeah, all the time. It's like I can't keep my brain on track. Like at the office or in my evening class, if a phone rings down the hall or I hear two people whispering in the back row, my attention just snaps right to that. Or even just my own thoughts, honestly. I'll be trying to read a spreadsheet and suddenly I'm wondering if I remembered to take the chicken out of the freezer for dinner. Which reminds me, I actually forgot to do that this morning. I'm going to have to stop at the store on the way home, which is the worst because the parking lot at that grocery store is always a nightmare around 5:30. People just abandon their carts wherever they want, and last week someone dinged my door. Just a little scratch, but it's a relatively new car, you know? Well, new to me, it's a 2018. But still. I was so mad. Have you ever had someone hit your car and just drive off without leaving a note? It's so inconsiderate. But um, yeah, my mind wanders constantly. Just any little noise or thought and I'm completely off track from what I was doing.

When your mind wanders like that, is it usually because outside noises or things around you are pulling your attention away, or is it more that you're stuck thinking about worries or concerns in your own head?

It's honestly both. Like I was saying, if I'm at the office or in my class, just one phone ringing down the hall or hearing people talking nearby is enough to completely pull me off what I was working on. But it's also just... my own head, you know? Like that random thought about the chicken. It's not usually big worries or anything, just random stuff. Like the other day, I was trying to type up these meeting minutes, and I suddenly started wondering whatever happened to my best friend from middle school. We used to be inseparable. We had these matching friendship bracelets that we made out of embroidery floss—do you remember those? We spent a whole summer making them on her back porch. Her mom used to bring us lemonade and those little windmill cookies. I haven't had one of those cookies in years. I wonder if they still make them? They always came in that crinkly cellophane package. Anyway, I ended up spending like twenty minutes looking her up on Facebook instead of finishing the minutes. She lives in Oregon now, apparently. Looks like she has a couple of dogs. I've always wanted a dog, but my apartment complex charges this ridiculous pet fee, and honestly, with how scatterbrained I am lately, I'd probably forget to walk it. But yeah, it's just... anything. A noise, a thought about a cookie... it just pulls me right away.

When you're trying to focus on something important, like work or studying, do you find it harder to ignore outside noises and distractions, or do you find it harder to stop your own worries and racing thoughts from taking over?

Well, I guess it's kind of like what I was just saying, it's really an equal mix of both. At the office or in my class, just one phone ringing or people talking nearby is enough to completely derail me. 

Actually, speaking of phones, we just got a new phone system at work last month and the default ringtone is so shrill. It's this awful electronic chirping noise. My boss refuses to figure out how to change the volume on his desk set, so it just echoes down the hall all day. He's not very good with technology anyway. Last week he asked me to fax an email. Fax an email! I had to explain to him that I could just forward it to the client. He's a nice guy, but sometimes I feel like I'm working in the 1990s. We still have these massive metal filing cabinets that take up half the break room, which is annoying because it means there's barely enough room for the microwave. And someone keeps microwaving fish on Tuesdays, which should honestly be illegal in an office setting. 

But anyway, yeah, the outside noise is definitely a huge distraction, but then it's also just those random thoughts about things at home pulling me off what I was working on. Like suddenly remembering I need to buy laundry detergent. I switched to those little detergent pods recently because the liquid always drips down the side of the bottle and makes the laundry room shelf all sticky. They're so much easier, though I always worry about dropping one and stepping on it. But um... yeah, honestly, I don't think one is harder to ignore than the other. Whether it's the phone ringing or a random thought about my laundry, they both just snap my attention right away from my work.

When you're in a quiet room by yourself with no distractions around you—like if you're alone at home trying to read something important—do you still have trouble keeping your attention on it, or is it mainly a problem when there are noises and other things going on around you?

Well, even when it's completely quiet, I still struggle. Like, if I'm at home alone and trying to read a long email from my landlord—which, by the way, he sends these massive emails about the most trivial things. Last week he sent three paragraphs about how we need to make sure the recycling is broken down properly because the city fined him. Which I get, but he could have just said "break down your boxes." But anyway, even in that quiet apartment, I'll read a sentence and then realize I'm thinking about whether I should paint my bathroom. The walls are this awful beige color right now, and I was looking at some paint swatches at Home Depot over the weekend. I was thinking maybe a soft blue? But then I remembered I'm renting, so I'd probably have to paint it back when I move out, and that just seems like a lot of work. Painting is so messy, you have to tape everything off and put down those drop cloths. I helped my sister paint her nursery a few years ago and we got paint all over the hardwood floor. It was a nightmare trying to scrape it off. So yeah, even without any noise, my brain just kind of... takes off on its own. I don't really need outside distractions to lose focus, honestly.

When you're doing something that you find really interesting or engaging—like watching one of those home renovation shows you mentioned, or something else you genuinely enjoy—do you still have trouble keeping your attention on it, or can you focus pretty well on things like that?

You know, it's funny you mention the home renovation shows, because I was actually just watching one last night. It was one of those where they buy a total fixer-upper, and this time they found this gorgeous old Victorian house. But the foundation was completely shot. They had to bring in these massive jacks to lift the whole house up—it was wild. I always wonder how much those people actually pay, because they always say their budget is like, fifty thousand dollars, and then they end up ripping out the entire kitchen and putting in custom marble countertops. Marble is so high maintenance, though. My aunt had marble in her kitchen and she said if you spill even a drop of lemon juice on it, it etches the surface and ruins the finish. She ended up having to get the whole thing resealed, which took days, and the smell of the sealant gave her a terrible migraine. She gets migraines a lot, actually. 

But um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, focusing on things I like. Um, I don't know, really. I mean, I guess I watch the shows, but I'm usually also scrolling on my phone or getting up to get a snack or something. I don't know if I'm really, like, locked in on them. I just kind of have them on.

Before you started the evening certificate program 15 months ago, when you were just working as a secretary without the extra classes, did you have these same kinds of attention and memory problems, or is this something that really started or got noticeably worse once you added the evening classes to your schedule?

Well, they've definitely been a lot harder to manage since I started that certificate program. It's been about 15 months now since I enrolled. I'm taking these classes in medical billing and coding because I really want to move up from just being a secretary, you know? It's a good field, supposedly lots of job security. My friend Sarah did a similar program, but for dental hygiene, and she makes really good money now. She just bought a new car, actually—one of those hybrid SUVs. It's really nice, it has those seats that heat up and cool down, which I didn't even know was a thing. I rode in it when we went to get lunch last week. We went to this new Thai place downtown, and I had the pad thai, but it was way too spicy. I usually love spicy food, but this was like, burning-my-mouth spicy. I had to drink three glasses of water just to get through it. The waiter kept looking at me funny because I kept asking for refills. 

But um, yeah, before the classes... I mean, I think I've always been a little scatterbrained, but trying to juggle the job and the evening classes is when it got really noticeably worse. It's just so much to keep track of now.

On days when you don't have your evening class and you have less going on, do you notice that your memory and concentration problems get better, or do they stay pretty much the same regardless of how busy you are?

Well, even on my days off from class, it's... I don't know, it's still pretty bad. Like, this past Saturday, I didn't have any classes, didn't have to work. I had the whole day to just catch up on things around the apartment. I made this whole list of chores I wanted to get done. I was going to do laundry, vacuum, and finally clean out my fridge because there's this weird smell coming from the back of it. I think it might be some leftover takeout from like, three weeks ago. I ordered from that Italian place down the street—the one with the really good garlic knots? Oh my gosh, their garlic knots are amazing. They drown them in butter and garlic, and they give you this little cup of marinara sauce that's just... perfect. My mom used to make homemade marinara sauce when I was a kid. She'd let it simmer on the stove all day Sunday, and the whole house would smell like tomatoes and basil. She tried to teach me how to make it once, but I always burn the garlic. If you burn garlic, it gets so bitter, you basically have to throw the whole pot out and start over. 

But um, what was I saying? Oh, right, my days off. Yeah, even when I have nothing going on, I still can't seem to focus. Like, I never actually got to the laundry or the fridge on Saturday. I just kind of bounced around doing half-finished things all day. So yeah, I don't think being less busy really helps much.

Have you had any recent illnesses, infections, or fevers in the past few months that you might not have mentioned? Or any changes in how you're sleeping at night—like trouble falling asleep, waking up a lot, or sleeping much more than usual?

No, no recent illnesses or anything like that. I haven't even had a cold this winter, which is honestly a miracle because usually I catch everything. The heating system in my apartment building is so old, it's constantly blowing this dry, dusty air everywhere. I bought one of those humidifiers to try and help, the kind that changes colors? It has this little tray where you can put essential oils. I tried putting eucalyptus oil in it because I read it's good for your sinuses, but I think I put way too many drops in because my whole bedroom smelled like a giant cough drop for three days. I had to keep the window open to air it out, which kind of defeated the purpose of having the heat on in the first place. My neighbor downstairs actually complained to the landlord that she was freezing because the draft from my window was coming down into her apartment. She complains about everything, though. Once she left a note on my door because she said my TV was too loud, but I wasn't even home! I was at the grocery store.

But um... wait, you asked about sleep, too, right? Yeah, my sleep is pretty much normal. I don't have trouble falling asleep or anything. I just go to bed and wake up like I usually do.

Over the past 15 months since your concentration problems started, has your ability to focus and remember things stayed pretty much the same day-to-day, or does it seem to get noticeably better or worse depending on the day or time of day?

Hmm, day-to-day... I don't really think there's a pattern. It feels pretty much the same no matter what time it is. Like, I thought maybe mornings were worse for a while, so I started going to this little coffee shop near my office to get an extra espresso shot before work. They have these amazing blueberry muffins, by the way. But they actually just changed the recipe last week. Now they put this chunky crystal sugar all over the top, and it makes a huge mess when you try to eat it at your desk. My coworker Janice was so mad about the crumb situation that she actually wrote a complaint email to their corporate office. 

Janice is always doing stuff like that, though. Last month she emailed our building manager because she said the toilet paper in the women's restroom was too scratchy. She literally brought in her own rolls from home and keeps them in her bottom desk drawer with her name written on the packaging in black Sharpie. She even bought the lavender-scented kind, which I personally think is a little weird for toilet paper, but whatever makes her happy, I guess. She's very particular about her desk area, too. She has all these little seasonal decorations she switches out. 

But um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, if my focus gets better or worse depending on the day. Yeah, no, I haven't really noticed it changing. It's just kind of always the same, whether it's morning or afternoon.
Have you ever felt confused about where you are, what time it is, or had trouble recognizing people around you? Or has anyone told you that you seemed confused or disoriented?

No, I don't think so. I always know where I am, and I definitely don't have trouble recognizing people. I'm actually really good with faces! Even if I forget someone's name, I never forget a face. Like, there's this delivery guy who brings packages to the front desk at my office, and I always recognize him before he even walks through the glass doors. 

He always wears the standard uniform, but he wears shorts, even in the middle of winter, which I just do not understand. But to make up for it, he wears these really loud, novelty socks pulled all the way up his calves. Last week he had on a pair with little tacos and hot sauce bottles all over them. It actually reminded me that I needed to figure out what to get my brother-in-law for his birthday, because he loves weird socks like that. He's completely impossible to shop for, honestly. He's one of those guys who just buys whatever he wants for himself on Amazon the second he thinks of it, so by the time his birthday rolls around, there's nothing left to get him. My sister usually just tells me to get him a gift card to this craft brewery near their house, but that feels so impersonal, you know? I hate giving gift cards. I like finding a gift that shows you actually thought about the person. Like, one year I spent hours tracking down this vintage vinyl record for him on eBay, and the shipping took forever because it came all the way from Germany...

But um, sorry, I completely lost my train of thought again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, about being confused. Yeah, no, I haven't had any issues like that. I know exactly where I am, and nobody has ever told me I seem disoriented or anything.

You mentioned the certificate program started about 15 months ago, which is when your memory and concentration problems got noticeably worse. Did anything else significant happen around that same time—like a major stressful event, a relationship change, a loss, or anything else emotionally difficult—or was it really just the classes that coincided with when you started noticing these problems?

No, there wasn't really any big dramatic event or anything like that. No breakups or anything. It really was just the classes. These attention and organization problems have just been noticeably harder to manage since I started the evening certificate program about 15 months ago. It's just a lot to juggle, you know? Because I work all day and then I have to drive straight over to the campus. 

The parking there is an absolute nightmare, by the way. They make you buy this expensive parking pass—it's like seventy-five dollars for the semester—but it doesn't even guarantee you a spot! You just have to drive around in circles for twenty minutes hoping someone leaves. And half the time, the people parked in the student lot aren't even taking classes. They're actually just going to that big chain gym across the street. You can totally tell because they're walking away from the campus in their workout gear, carrying those giant gallon water jugs. I really don't get the gallon water jug trend, honestly. It seems so heavy to carry around all day. 

My coworker Janice—the one with the toilet paper I was telling you about?—she bought one of those jugs, but hers has these little motivational quotes printed on the side for every hour. Like "Keep chugging!" and "You're almost there!" She left it on the breakroom counter once and it leaked everywhere because she didn't screw the lid on right, and it completely ruined a stack of mail I had just sorted for the outgoing bin. I had to reprint all the labels, and the tape wouldn't stick to the wet envelopes... 

But um, wait, I'm sorry, I lost track again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, if anything else stressful happened. But yeah, no, nothing else was going on. Just the certificate program starting up.

Have you started taking any new medications, supplements, or over-the-counter drugs in the past 15 months—even something you might think is minor? And have you noticed any changes in how much caffeine, alcohol, or anything else you might be consuming?

No, I haven't started any new medications or anything like that. I don't really take supplements either. My mom is always trying to get me to take these huge fish oil pills, though. She swears by them for everything—joints, memory, whatever. She orders them from this catalogue that comes in the mail, which I think is so funny because who orders from catalogues anymore? But she refuses to put her credit card into a computer. 

She still writes checks for her groceries, too. The cashiers at her local grocery store all know her by name because she holds up the line filling out her checkbook. But anyway, she gave me a bottle of those fish oil pills for Christmas last year, wrapped up in my stocking. They were so big I couldn't even swallow them, and they smelled awful. I ended up throwing them away when she wasn't looking. I felt a little bad, but honestly, I think most of those vitamins just give you really expensive pee. 

My dog, though, he takes these little joint supplements that look like treats. They're bacon-flavored. He's getting older—he's a beagle mix, about ten years old—and he was starting to limp a little when he got up from his bed. The vet recommended them, and they've actually worked wonders. He's back to chasing squirrels in the backyard like he's a puppy. He almost caught one yesterday, but it scurried up the oak tree just in time. The squirrels in our neighborhood are so bold, though. They'll just sit on the fence and stare at him...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, medications and caffeine and stuff. Yeah, no new meds or supplements for me. And my caffeine and drinking habits are pretty much exactly the same as they've always been. Just my regular coffee in the morning and maybe a glass of wine on the weekends, but nothing has changed.

In the past 15 months, has there ever been a time when you suddenly felt confused, foggy, or like your thinking was really off—like it came on pretty quickly over hours or a day or two, rather than gradually over weeks?

No, definitely not. It hasn't been a sudden thing where I just wake up and feel completely foggy or out of it. It's really just been a steady kind of struggling to keep up with everything. 

Though, speaking of foggy, my car windshield was completely fogged up yesterday morning, and my defroster is totally broken. I had to sit in my driveway for like fifteen minutes with the windows rolled down in the freezing cold just waiting for it to clear so I could drive to work. I really need to take it into the shop, but my regular mechanic, Dave, just retired. He moved down to Florida, which I totally get because the winters here are brutal, but now I have to find a new guy. My neighbor recommended this place over on 4th Street, but I looked them up on Yelp and someone left a review saying the guys there stole the loose change out of their cup holder! Which, honestly, who steals quarters? I keep a little stack of them in my car for the parking meters downtown, because the city's parking app never works right on my phone. It always freezes right when I'm trying to hit the confirm button, and then you don't know if you paid or not, so you have to check your bank statement...

But um... wait. Sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? What was the question? Oh, right, if my brain ever got suddenly foggy over a day or two. No, nothing sudden like that. Just the same old distraction stuff I've been dealing with since the classes started.
Have you had any recent infections, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, or anything like that in the past few months—even something mild that you might have treated at home?

No, I haven't had any infections or anything like that. No UTIs or pneumonia. Although, speaking of UTIs, somebody at work keeps leaving these massive bottles of cranberry juice in the office mini-fridge. Like, the really huge ones that take up the entire bottom shelf. It's so annoying because then nobody else has room for their lunch bags. I usually bring a salad in one of those glass Tupperware containers—you know the ones with the snap-on lids? They're amazing because they never stain if you put spaghetti sauce in them, unlike the plastic ones. 

I actually threw out all my plastic containers last year after I read this article about microplastics. It's really terrifying what's in everything now. Even the tap water at the office tastes kind of metallic, which is why everyone is so obsessed with bringing their own drinks, like Janice and that leaky motivational jug I was telling you about. The building management said they were going to change the water filter in the breakroom back in October, but they never did. Getting maintenance to do anything in that building is like pulling teeth. You have to put in a work order online, but the portal is always down for maintenance itself, which is kind of ironic if you think about it... 

Oh gosh, wait. I'm rambling again, aren't I? I am so sorry. What did you ask me? Right, infections. No, I haven't been sick at all lately. I've been totally healthy.

You mentioned your concentration problems have been pretty much the same day-to-day since they started 15 months ago. But I want to make sure I'm understanding correctly—when you're in the middle of your workday, does your ability to focus stay about the same throughout the day, or do you notice it gets noticeably better or worse at certain times, like maybe worse in the afternoon or evening?

Well, I'd say it's pretty much the same all day. I don't really notice a difference between the morning or the afternoon. It's just a constant struggle to stay on task. 

Although, speaking of the afternoon, that's usually when the snack cart comes around at work. It's this little metal cart that one of the building ladies pushes around, and the wheels squeak so loudly you can hear it coming from all the way down the hall. It sounds exactly like this squeaky toy my dog used to have. It was a little rubber chicken, and he loved it so much he carried it everywhere. He even tried to bury it in the couch cushions once and ended up ripping a hole in the upholstery. My husband was so mad because we had just bought that couch. We got it at this big Labor Day sale at the furniture store out on Route 9. 

The traffic out there is always a nightmare, though, especially on holiday weekends. People drive like absolute maniacs. I swear nobody uses their turn signals anymore. I was driving behind this guy the other day, and he just slammed on his brakes and swerved into the turning lane without any warning at all. I had to hit my brakes so hard my purse flew off the passenger seat and everything spilled out onto the floor. My lip gloss rolled all the way under the seat, and I still haven't been able to fish it out. It's my favorite shade, too—this really nice berry color that I get from the drugstore...

Oh, wait. I'm so sorry. I did it again. You were asking about my focus during the day, right? Yeah, it doesn't really get better or worse at any specific time. It's just consistently bad all day long.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sudden onset of confusion or cognitive impairment (delirium), which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, definitely not. It hasn't been a sudden thing where I just wake up and feel completely foggy or out of it. It's really just been a steady kind of struggling to keep up with everything. 

Though, speaking of foggy, my car windshield was completely fogged up yesterday morning, and my defroster is totally broken. I had to sit in my driveway for like fifteen minutes with the windows rolled down in the freezing cold just waiting for it to clear so I could drive to work. I really need to take it into the shop, but my regular mechanic, Dave, just retired. He moved down to Florida, which I totally get because the winters here are brutal, but now I have to find a new guy. My neighbor recommended this place over on 4th Street, but I looked them up on Yelp and someone left a review saying the guys there stole the loose change out of their cup holder! Which, honestly, who steals quarters? I keep a little stack of them in my car for the parking meters downtown, because the city's parking app never works right on my phone. It always freezes right when I'm trying to hit the confirm button, and then you don't know if you paid or not, so you have to check your bank statement...

But um... wait. Sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? What was the question? Oh, right, if my brain ever got suddenly foggy over a day or two. No, nothing sudden like that. Just the same old distraction stuff I've been dealing with since the classes started.

doctor.intent: Determine if cognitive symptoms are attributable to a medical/neurological condition (delirium from infection/metabolic cause) versus a primary psychiatric or adjustment disorder. Need to assess for acute medical illness that could cause delirium.
doctor.question: Have you had any recent infections, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, or anything like that in the past few months—even something mild that you might have treated at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recent infections or illnesses, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't had any infections or anything like that. No UTIs or pneumonia. Although, speaking of UTIs, somebody at work keeps leaving these massive bottles of cranberry juice in the office mini-fridge. Like, the really huge ones that take up the entire bottom shelf. It's so annoying because then nobody else has room for their lunch bags. I usually bring a salad in one of those glass Tupperware containers—you know the ones with the snap-on lids? They're amazing because they never stain if you put spaghetti sauce in them, unlike the plastic ones. 

I actually threw out all my plastic containers last year after I read this article about microplastics. It's really terrifying what's in everything now. Even the tap water at the office tastes kind of metallic, which is why everyone is so obsessed with bringing their own drinks, like Janice and that leaky motivational jug I was telling you about. The building management said they were going to change the water filter in the breakroom back in October, but they never did. Getting maintenance to do anything in that building is like pulling teeth. You have to put in a work order online, but the portal is always down for maintenance itself, which is kind of ironic if you think about it... 

Oh gosh, wait. I'm rambling again, aren't I? I am so sorry. What did you ask me? Right, infections. No, I haven't been sick at all lately. I've been totally healthy.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has delirium (acute onset with fluctuating course) versus a primary psychiatric or anxiety disorder, by asking about the temporal pattern and consistency of symptoms across the day
doctor.question: You mentioned your concentration problems have been pretty much the same day-to-day since they started 15 months ago. But I want to make sure I'm understanding correctly—when you're in the middle of your workday, does your ability to focus stay about the same throughout the day, or do you notice it gets noticeably better or worse at certain times, like maybe worse in the afternoon or evening?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fluctuations in the ability to focus throughout the day, which is checking for a fluctuating course often seen in conditions like delirium. My symptom profile does not include a specific item for fluctuating attention.

patient.answer:
Well, I'd say it's pretty much the same all day. I don't really notice a difference between the morning or the afternoon. It's just a constant struggle to stay on task. 

Although, speaking of the afternoon, that's usually when the snack cart comes around at work. It's this little metal cart that one of the building ladies pushes around, and the wheels squeak so loudly you can hear it coming from all the way down the hall. It sounds exactly like this squeaky toy my dog used to have. It was a little rubber chicken, and he loved it so much he carried it everywhere. He even tried to bury it in the couch cushions once and ended up ripping a hole in the upholstery. My husband was so mad because we had just bought that couch. We got it at this big Labor Day sale at the furniture store out on Route 9. 

The traffic out there is always a nightmare, though, especially on holiday weekends. People drive like absolute maniacs. I swear nobody uses their turn signals anymore. I was driving behind this guy the other day, and he just slammed on his brakes and swerved into the turning lane without any warning at all. I had to hit my brakes so hard my purse flew off the passenger seat and everything spilled out onto the floor. My lip gloss rolled all the way under the seat, and I still haven't been able to fish it out. It's my favorite shade, too—this really nice berry color that I get from the drugstore...

Oh, wait. I'm so sorry. I did it again. You were asking about my focus during the day, right? Yeah, it doesn't really get better or worse at any specific time. It's just consistently bad all day long.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a 15-month history of cognitive complaints (memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, distractibility) that began coinciding with enrollment in an evening certificate program. Notably, there is no evidence of mood disorder (denies sadness, anxiety, or depression), no psychotic symptoms, no trauma history, and no significant psychosocial stressor beyond the normal demands of her job and studies. The pattern of attention difficulties occurring in the context of increased workload, combined with the absence of mood symptoms and the patient's characteristic tangential, rambling speech pattern throughout the interview (suggesting possible baseline personality features rather than acute psychiatric illness), points toward a neurocognitive concern. Given the acute onset 15 months ago without prior head injury, infection, or medication changes reported, and the persistent nature despite reduced workload on days off, F06.7 (Unspecified disorder of adult personality and behavior) is considered, though the presentation is atypical. However, the most parsimonious diagnosis given the clinical picture is adjustment-related cognitive complaints. The differential includes F32.9 (Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified) and F41.1 (Generalized anxiety disorder), though mood and anxiety symptoms were explicitly denied.
